fields.Front: You are told: 'In an inventory system, a Warehouse class holds stock, prints shipping labels, and emails suppliers.' What design flaw is this and how do you fix it?
fields.Back: Low cohesion: three unrelated responsibilities in one module, so a change to label printing forces retesting of stock logic. Split into Warehouse (stock), LabelPrinter, and SupplierNotifier, restoring high cohesion and following the Single Responsibility Principle.

fields.Front: A Customer object holds a reference to its Order objects and both exist independently. Which Week 1 relationship is this?
fields.Back: Association: the objects know about each other. If the Order could not exist without the Customer and were contained by it, it would be aggregation instead.

fields.Front: Admin and RegularUser both need login() and changePassword(), and Admin adds banUser(). Which relationship, and why?
fields.Back: Inheritance: each is a specialized version of a common User class. Put the shared attributes and methods in User and let Admin add its own, which reduces duplication and creates a hierarchy.

fields.Front: Given code that mutates a shared object from two threads and now has race conditions, which paradigm's strength does this illustrate and why?
fields.Back: FP's: concurrency is hard in OOP precisely because of shared mutable state (race conditions, deadlocks, difficult debugging, locks needed). In FP data is immutable after creation, so multiple threads can read it without interference and there is nothing to lock.

fields.Front: You remove = 0 from virtual void draw() = 0; in Shape. What changes?
fields.Back: draw() becomes an ordinary virtual function, so Shape is no longer abstract and CAN be instantiated. It now needs a body or you get a linker error, and subclasses are no longer required to provide their own draw().

fields.Front: You remove virtual from void draw() in Shape and hold a Shape* pointing at a Circle. What does p->draw() call?
fields.Back: Shape::draw(). Without virtual the call is resolved statically from the pointer's declared type, so the derived override is never reached and polymorphism is lost. override in Circle would also become a compile error.

fields.Front: You remove const from double getBalance() const and a caller holds const Account& a. What happens?
fields.Back: a.getBalance() no longer compiles: a non-const member function cannot be called on a const object or const reference. Marking read-only methods const is what keeps them usable from const contexts.

fields.Front: A team wants to add a fourth payment type to a system where every caller writes if (type == CREDIT) ... else if (type == PAYPAL) .... Which OOP advantage is being wasted?
fields.Back: Polymorphism (and with it extensibility). A PaymentMethod interface with CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, CryptoPayment implementations lets a new type be added without touching the processing logic; the if-chain must be edited in every caller.

fields.Front: You need to unit-test an Order class that talks to a live Payment gateway. Which Week 1 advantage and which technique apply?
fields.Back: Debugging and Testing: classes are self-contained units testable in isolation. Use a mock object or dependency injection to substitute a fake Payment (and Shipping) so the test never touches the real gateway.

fields.Front: Classify: a module is internally focused on one job but imports and calls six other modules directly. Which of the four combinations is this?
fields.Back: High cohesion + high coupling: internally well-organized but with strong dependencies, so changes still ripple between modules.

fields.Front: Given int applyFunction(int x, int y, int (*func)(int,int)), what must you write to also support a lambda that captures a variable?
fields.Back: Change the parameter to std::function<int(int,int)>. A raw function pointer cannot hold a capturing lambda; std::function wraps any callable with the right signature.

fields.Front: A stakeholder says the system 'must model payroll entities with attributes and behaviours and track their state over time'. Which paradigm fits, and why?
fields.Back: OOP: the slides list business systems such as payroll and inventory, user interfaces, and games as typical OOP use cases, because the system maps naturally to real-world entities and managing mutable state is critical.

fields.Front: Someone writes Car myCar; for the slides' Car class. Why does it fail?
fields.Back: Car declares only Car(std::string, int), so no default constructor is generated once a user-defined constructor exists. You must supply both arguments, e.g. Car myCar("Toyota", 2022);.

fields.Front: Which is 5 * 2 then squared, and which is 5 squared then doubled: squareNumber(doubleNumber(5)) or doubleNumber(squareNumber(5))? Give both results.
fields.Back: squareNumber(doubleNumber(5)) doubles first: 10 then 100. doubleNumber(squareNumber(5)) squares first: 25 then 50. Evaluation is inside-out, so the innermost call runs first.

fields.Front: A class declares protected: int hitPoints;. Which code can touch it?
fields.Back: The class's own member functions and any derived class's member functions. Code outside the hierarchy cannot, unlike public; derived classes can, unlike private.

fields.Front: You are told an e-commerce team wants Payment bugs fixed without retesting ShoppingCart and Order. Which advantage and which underlying idea does this rely on?
fields.Back: Maintainability, which rests on separation of concerns: each class is responsible for a specific part of the system, so changes are isolated to a single class and modifying one part typically does not affect others.
